units.translation: v. Forty days: the days of the Etesian winds some say are forty, others fifty, as Timosthenes (fg 7 E. A. Wagner Die Erdbeschreibung des T., Diss. Lips. 1888, 67). They begin to blow when the sun is at the end of Cancer, blow through all of Leo, and cease in the second degree of Virgo.

w. And still now on Ceos sacred: for he legislated for the Ceans to watch annually with arms for the rising of the Dog Star and to sacrifice to it. Hence the Etesian winds blow, cooling the earth in summer, and the Greeks were relieved of drought. L
528-29a. Are sung: are sung, are said. Lg P
b. But the chieftains there: for the Etesian winds are contrary to those sailing into the Pontus, being north winds in those regions, just as in Greece they are contrary to the west winds.

531-32. An altar on the shore opposite: on the opposite shore, he says, of Asia, having sailed across to it, they built an altar to the twelve gods. It is clear, then, that it is in Europe; for even now there is a sanctuary so called on the opposite side of Europe [of Asia]. Timosthenes (fg 28 E. A. Wagner Die Erdbeschreibung des T., Diss. Lips. 1888, 69) says that the sons of Phrixus set up an altar of the twelve gods, but the Argonauts one of Poseidon. Herodorus (31 fg 47 J.) says that the Argonauts sacrificed on the altar on which Argus, son of Phrixus, had sacrificed on his return. The twelve gods are these:
Zeus, Poseidon, Hades, Hermes, Hephaestus, Apollo, Demeter, Hera, Hestia, Artemis, Aphrodite, and Athena.
533-36a. Nor the dove: they did not forget the dove. The order: but Euphemus held it in his hand. L
b. δῆμα is written and δεῖμα. Written with η it means bond, with the diphthong fear. P

541-48a. As when someone from his homeland: the simile is taken from Homer (O 80): 'as when the mind of a man darts'. The sense: just as, when someone wandering from his homeland—as often happens to men—sees in his thought his own home, the intervening distance does not seem great to him, but all the cities are visible, and at the same time the road to his own land by land and sea appears to him, and now here, now there, from the place where he is, he swiftly traverses it with his eyes, having his thought in rapid motion, so swiftly did Athena pass through the intervening land and arrive at the Cyanean rocks.
b. The word ἀλώμενος must be referred to ἐνόησεν. In πλαζόμεθα τετληότες a transposition must be made, as πλαζόμενοι τέτλαμεν. P
c. Nor any far-off land: nor does the distance of any land seem great to him.
